content:
Steroids such as prednisolone work quickly to calm inflammation, but they can cause side effects. Short courses usually cause mild, temporary effects such as raised appetite, poor sleep or mood changes. Long-term use can thin bones, raise blood sugar and blood pressure, and increase infection risk. Never stop steroid tablets suddenly after more than a few weeks; your doctor will reduce them gradually.

How steroids are used in arthritis

Steroids, also called corticosteroids, are man-made versions of a hormone your body makes naturally. In arthritis they may be given:

  • as tablets, often prednisolone, for flares or while slower medicines start working
  • as an injection into a joint, to settle one painful, swollen joint
  • as an injection into a muscle, to calm a widespread flare
  • as infusions in hospital, occasionally

For rheumatoid arthritis, NICE (NG100) advises using steroids as short-term bridging treatment and keeping long-term use to a minimum.

Common short-term side effects

  • increased appetite and weight gain
  • difficulty sleeping
  • mood changes, feeling restless, low or irritable
  • indigestion or heartburn. Taking tablets with food in the morning can help.
  • raised blood sugar, especially important if you have diabetes

These usually settle when the dose comes down.

Possible long-term side effects

  • thinner bones (osteoporosis) and higher fracture risk
  • higher blood pressure and blood sugar, sometimes triggering diabetes
  • infections that are more frequent or more serious
  • weight gain around the face and tummy
  • thinning skin and easy bruising
  • muscle weakness, especially in the thighs
  • eye problems such as cataracts or glaucoma

The risk rises with higher doses and longer use. Your doctor will weigh this against the harm uncontrolled inflammation can cause.

Protecting your bones

NICE (CG146) recommends a fracture risk assessment for people taking steroid tablets for three months or more. Your GP may suggest bone-protecting treatment, calcium and vitamin D, or a DEXA scan. Weight-bearing exercise and not smoking also help.

Never stop suddenly

If you take steroid tablets for more than three weeks, your body's own steroid production can switch off. Stopping suddenly can cause a dangerous drop, called adrenal crisis. Your doctor will reduce the dose slowly. You may be given a steroid emergency card. Carry it and show it if you become unwell, need surgery or visit A&E. If you are vomiting and cannot keep tablets down, get medical advice the same day.

Steroid injections into a joint

Joint injections usually cause fewer whole-body effects, but you may notice:

  • a flare of pain for a day or two afterwards
  • flushing of the face
  • a temporary rise in blood sugar if you have diabetes
  • rarely, a small dent or pale patch in the skin at the site

There is a small risk of infection. If the joint becomes hot, red, more swollen and more painful in the days after an injection, especially with fever, seek urgent help. Most people are advised to limit how many injections a joint has each year.

Infections and chickenpox

Steroids can make infections harder to fight. Tell your doctor if you develop a fever or feel unwell. If you have never had chickenpox or shingles and come into contact with someone who has it, contact your GP promptly, as you may need treatment.

Reporting side effects

Tell your GP, pharmacist or rheumatology team about any side effects. You can also report them to the MHRA through the Yellow Card scheme.

Questions to ask your doctor

  • Why do I need steroids, and for how long?
  • How will the dose be reduced?
  • Do I need bone protection or a bone density scan?
  • Should my blood pressure or blood sugar be checked more often?
  • Do I need a steroid emergency card?

Writing your questions down before an appointment makes it easier to get the answers you need.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
